title: Terminal-Optimal Graph Diffusion with Null-Model-Constrained and Structure-Preserving Noise
abstract: Graph diffusion models have emerged as a promising approach for generating complex networks, yet they typically face two major drawbacks. First, terminating the forward process in pure Gaussian noise eliminates the intrinsic structural signatures of the original network, which leads to suboptimal generation quality. Second, the absence of constraints along the diffusion trajectory causes progressive degradation of topological features, ultimately resulting in complete structural collapse. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Null-Model-Constrained Graph Diffusion (NMC-GD), a principled framework incorporating specialized designs for graph generation. Specifically, we substitute the conventional isotropic prior with a null-model distribution as the new forward diffusion endpoint, explicitly preserving critical statistical properties of the network. In addition, we develop a null-model-guided continuous-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) and design a directional noise term that enforces a global structural constraint on the diffusion trajectory, striking a balance between stochasticity and structural invariance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that NMC-GD achieves superior generation quality and computational efficiency.

title: TRACE: Tracing Temporal Constraints for Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
abstract: Complex temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA) requires composing multiple time-dependent facts under constraints such as validity intervals, temporal ordering, overlap, and set-style operations. Recent LLM-based approaches improve temporal reasoning through retrieval, decomposition, or planning, but the temporal constraints produced during intermediate reasoning are often left implicit: retrieved evidence may be temporally invalid, intermediate answers may be propagated without verification, and deterministic temporal operations may still be handled by free-form generation. We propose TRACE, a temporal-constraint-aware recursive framework that traces temporal constraints across retrieval, answer verification, constraint propagation, and execution. TRACE grounds temporal anchors and operators from sub-questions and intermediate answers, performs operator-aware temporal retrieval, verifies child-derived answers using grounding, bridge evidence, and operator consistency, and invokes symbolic temporal execution when root-level temporal operations are deterministically resolvable. Experiments on MultiTQ and TimelineKGQA show that TRACE improves multi-step and operator-sensitive temporal reasoning under the evaluated settings. Detailed analyses further show that verified answer propagation reduces error accumulation, while symbolic temporal execution is particularly effective for compositional temporal relations such as intersection and union. These results demonstrate that complex TKGQA benefits not only from retrieving or decomposing temporal questions, but also from explicitly tracing, verifying, and executing temporal constraints throughout the reasoning process.

title: Text-Conditioned Scene Graph Sequence Generation via Discrete Diffusion
abstract: Scene graphs represent visual scenes as objects and their relationships. While considerable research has explored predicting scene graph sequences from images or videos, generating such sequences from text remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce a discrete diffusion framework for text-conditioned scene graph sequence generation, focusing on visual scenes centered on human--object interactions. The proposed framework represents each sequence as a fixed-slot discrete state, where each slot encodes the state of an object over time, and employs a Transformer-based denoiser to generate scene graph sequences aligned with the input text. The denoiser jointly leverages within-frame slot attention, cross-frame temporal attention, and text cross-attention to capture inter-object relationships, temporal dynamics, and text--graph correspondence. We compare the proposed framework with diverse baselines, including retrieval-based methods, scene graph parsers, large language models, sequence-to-sequence models, and non-diffusion generative models. Experimental results show that our framework improves both text--graph alignment and the accuracy of temporal dynamics represented in scene graph sequences, including object appearance, persistence, and disappearance.

title: Learning to Act, Failing to Retrieve: Diagnosing Reward-Effectiveness Mismatch in Proactive Conversational Information Retrieval
abstract: Proactive conversational information retrieval (CIR) requires an agent to decide not only what to retrieve, but how to act: when to ask the user for clarification, when to issue a new retrieval, and when to reuse evidence it has already gathered. We study this as a sequential dialogue-management problem over Ask, Push, and Reuse. We train the interaction policy with reinforcement learning in an LLM-driven environment providing user simulation, query reformulation, and a relevance judge that scores the training reward; evaluation instead uses held-out human relevance judgements (qrels). The resulting agent learns coherent, state-dependent behaviour and accumulates high shaped reward, yet its qrel-based retrieval effectiveness (nDCG, MAP) falls at or below simple non-learned baselines on iKAT. We argue that this reflects a reward–effectiveness mismatch: the shaped reward, scored by an LLM judge and crediting cheap reuse of buffered evidence, is only loosely coupled to held-out qrel effectiveness. We localize this mismatch to reward design and show that replacing the dialogue-shaped signal with a retrieval-gain-aligned reward recovers much of the gap to the strongest non-learned baseline—roughly doubling nDCG@10 and MAP, with the residual gap traced to clarification quality—suggesting that reward formulation is a key lever for aligning proactive dialogue behaviour with retrieval quality.

title: SEMAPHORE: Semantic Detour over Incomplete Knowledge Graphs for Multi-hop Numerical QA
abstract: Numerical question answering (QA) over Knowledge Graphs (KGs) requires retrieving numerical values from structured sources. Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) and KG-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) methods exploit multi-hop connectivity for entity-centric questions but remain brittle for numerical queries, whose values typically appear as sparse attribute leaves. When required triples are missing, target values can become unreachable by explicit traversal; structural methods may retrieve values from the wrong numerical attribute, while numerical solvers assuming directly attached values cannot access non-local evidence. We propose SEMAPHORE, a neuro-symbolic framework that reformulates numerical QA over KGs as a semantic detour problem. SEMAPHORE combines symbolic path planning with embedding-based geometric navigation and decoupled scoring that separates relational navigation from numerical attribute grounding. This design identifies plausible detours while preserving the metric semantics required for accurate numerical answers. On numerical QA benchmarks derived from FB15K-237 and YAGO15K, SEMAPHORE outperforms strong LLM and KG-augmented baselines, demonstrating the value of semantic detours for robust numerical knowledge access over KGs. Sparsity and cross-dataset transfer experiments show that this advantage persists under severe graph incompleteness and when target-specific Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) training is replaced with transferred schema embeddings. Code is available at https://github.com/orcies8147/SEMAPHORE.

title: Amplified and Emergent Safety Risks in Multi-Agent Recommendation and Retrieval
abstract: Recommendation and retrieval systems are increasingly built by composition, with pipelines of LLM-powered agents that retrieve, reason, and act replacing standalone models. This shift inherits long-standing risks while introducing new ones, yet the resulting threats to robustness and safety, and the strategies to contain them, remain underexplored. Focusing on multi-agent recommender systems, this tutorial organises these threats along three tiers, from drift through misalignment to compromise, and separates risks that composition merely amplifies from those that emerge only once agents interact. Because agents that each pass their own safety checks can still interact in unsafe ways, we also show how to scope evaluation to the level at which each failure surfaces: the individual agent, the interaction, or the composed system. Interactive walkthroughs of simulated attacks illustrate how these failures propagate through complete recommender and retrieval pipelines.

title: LLMTGL: Large Language Models for Robust Text-Attributed Graph Learning under Missing Text and Label Noise
abstract: Text-attributed graphs have attracted considerable attention due to their extensive applications in domains such as social networks and citation networks. Existing methods typically rely on reliable text-attributed graphs. However, the frequent occurrence of missing text in real-world scenarios severely constrains model performance. Meanwhile, label noise is inevitably introduced during the data annotation process, leading to a degradation in the performance of graph learning. The large language model (LLM), with their text generation and semantic understanding, offers a unified solution to the challenges of missing text and label noise. To jointly address both challenges, we propose LLMTGL, a novel graph learning framework for text-attributed graph node classification. Specifically, we introduce graph topological properties to construct augmented prompts that guide the LLM in generating semantically coherent academic text descriptions for nodes with missing text. Subsequently, we design an LLM-driven pseudo-label expansion mechanism that selects high-confidence unlabeled nodes to the training set. This framework jointly optimizes for missing text and label noise by integrating graph topological structure with semantic information. Experimental results demonstrate that LLMTGL achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on text-missing graphs with noisy labels. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLMTGL-EC24ssjs.

title: Can Frontier LLMs Capture $40 Billion in Supply Chain Value?
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on many NLP tasks, but their ability to reason about complex supply chain relationships remains unclear. We introduce the Supply Chain Intuition Exam (SCIE), a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can identify and infer direct and indirect supplier relationships. We compare standard LLMs, models with grounding-based retrieval, and deep research (DR) systems. Despite access to public financial reports and real-world data, recall remains low: standard and grounded models achieve approximately 3--16%, while the best DR systems reach only 22%. These results suggest that retrieval alone is insufficient for professional-grade supply chain reasoning. SCIE highlights the need for methods that better integrate domain knowledge, retrieval, and multi-step reasoning in business and finance applications.

title: POLAR: Policy Optimization through Larger Reasoners
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a practical way to improve the reasoning and decision-making abilities of large language models, but its training signal is often sparse. When a policy faces prompts beyond its current ability, every sampled trajectory in a group may fail the verifier, resulting in an all-zero group. In this case, group-relative policy optimization gives little useful gradient even when the prompt contains valuable learning content. This capacity-difficulty mismatch is especially costly for smaller models used in knowledge-intensive and web-interaction tasks. We present POLAR, a difficulty-aware training framework that augments on-policy RL with conditional guidance from a larger reasoner. POLAR uses the standard GRPO branch when at least one sampled response succeeds, and switches to a supervised objective over verified teacher trajectories only when the whole student group receives zero reward. The method can turn otherwise wasted all-zero groups into targeted learning opportunities while keeping policy exploration on prompts the student can handle. We formalize the switching criterion, teacher selection objective, mixed RL/supervised loss, and compute overhead. We evaluate POLAR on WebShop, GAIA, and WebWalkerQA using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B policies. The results show consistent gains over matched GRPO baselines, with large improvements on hard web traversal questions for the two smaller policies. Ablations and diagnostics further show that the gains come from the proposed all-zero recovery mechanism.

title: PRISM: Reliable LLM Knowledge Distillation from Graph-Context Perspectives for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
abstract: Text-attributed graph (TAG) learning aims to leverage both textual attributes and graph structures for node classification. Recent studies have utilized Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate pseudo-labels and rationales for few-label TAG learning. However, existing approaches typically rely solely on the textual attribute of target nodes, making the generated knowledge susceptible to noise and unreliability. To address this limitation, we propose PRISM (Perspective-based Reliable Imitation with Semantic Multiplicity), a reliability-aware knowledge distillation framework for few-label TAG learning. PRISM constructs multiple structural-context perspectives for each target node and estimates the reliability of LLM-generated knowledge based on cross-perspective consistency. The resulting reliability weights are then incorporated into the distillation process, enabling GNNs to place greater emphasis on more reliable supervision signals. Extensive experiments on five TAG benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms existing methods in few-label node classification.

title: Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning for LLM Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are fundamental for grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in factually consistent reasoning across diverse data-mining tasks. However, when reasoning over complex graph topologies, LLMs can be brittle in maintaining structural consistency and may rely on spurious correlations. We propose SKILL (Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning), a novel paradigm that transforms relational rules from passive symbolic patterns into explicit, generation-time symbolic guidance for LLM-based reasoning. Unlike existing methods that isolate symbolic mining from neural inference, SKILL introduces a semantically aligned rule synthesis framework that filters spurious patterns and enables LLMs to leverage relational regularities during inference. By grounding generation in pruned, query-specific subgraph structures together with rule–path evidence, SKILL improves inductive generalization while preserving generative flexibility. Extensive experiments on three inductive benchmarks demonstrate that SKILL achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to a 5% absolute improvement in Hits@1, highlighting a new and effective way to integrate symbolic structure into LLM reasoning over knowledge graphs. Source code is available at https://github.com/luilui97/SKILL.

title: SymGRPO: Preventing Mode Collapse in Group Relative Policy Optimization via Symmetric Anti-Reinforcement
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become the dominant critic-free method for reinforcement learning from human feedback in large language models, with growing adoption for fine-tuning LLM-based retrievers, query reformulators, rerankers, and agentic search systems. We identify a fundamental failure mode of GRPO in multi-prompt training: prompt-blind mode collapse, where the policy converges to a single output regardless of input prompt—a critical concern for information retrieval applications where prompt-conditioned behavior is essential. We prove this arises from a quadratic gradient vanishing at the collapsed state: GRPO's entropy restoration rate is Θ(ε2|log ε|) where ε = 1 − πmax. We propose SymGRPO, which augments GRPO with an anti-reinforcement log-barrier on unchosen tokens, raising the restoration rate to Θ(ε|log ε|)—a diverging ratio of α(V − 1)/ε. Critically, this benefit appears only when the batch advantage sum S ≠ 0, which holds under EMA baselines but is forced to zero by standard mean-zero normalization. Across four small-scale reasoning tasks, GRPO mode-collapses to 19–50% accuracy while SymGRPO reaches 100% on multi-solution tasks. The modification is three lines of code.

title: Group-Relative RL Post-Training for Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Sequential recommender systems are typically trained with next-item cross-entropy (CE), yet evaluated by top-N ranking metrics that reward relative item ordering in the recommendation slate. This mismatch remains unaddressed for strong collaborative sequential models. Recent group-relative reinforcement learning has shown promise for LLM alignment and LLM-based recommenders, but whether a critic-free post-training paradigm can reliably improve standard collaborative sequential recommenders remains unclear. We introduce GRFT (Group-Relative Fine-Tuning), a GRPO-style post-training framework that aligns a pretrained sequential recommender directly to slate-level ranking rewards. GRFT samples multiple top-K slates per user context via Plackett-Luce sampling without replacement, scores them with ranking rewards, and updates the model with a PPO-clipped group-relative objective anchored to the frozen supervised reference. We instantiate rankwise and listwise variants to support position-level and whole-slate credit assignment. Under leakage-resistant global temporal splits on four datasets, GRFT consistently improves a strong sequential backbone, achieving gains of up to 25.3% NDCG@20 and 19.5% Recall@20. The improvements remain complementary to stronger supervised initialization, showing that reward-aligned post-training adds value beyond better supervised training alone. GRFT thus establishes that GRPO-style, critic-free post-training can improve strong collaborative sequential recommenders.

title: ACMDG: An Effective and Scalable Active Clustering via Multi-granularity Diffusion Graph
abstract: Active clustering injects minimal human feedback into clustering via pairwise constraints, which is highly useful in data mining pipelines but difficult to scale in practice. Existing methods are expensive in two stages: initialization often requires building costly global structures, and each interaction round may trigger heavy recomputation. Meanwhile, substantial accuracy gains still demand many constraints. We present ACMDG, an effective and scalable active clustering framework built on a multi-granularity diffusion graph. ACMDG constructs a sparse yet connected multi-granularity diffusion graph structure by progressively modeling data relationships from fine-grained nearest-neighbor links to coarse-grained representations. Within an iterative refinement framework, it selects informative nodes in batch mode, categorizes them efficiently via a neighborhood-set-based interaction strategy, and refines clustering by diffusion-based label propagation. The overall framework runs in O(n log n) time. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets show that ACMDG outperforms its counterparts in most cases in terms of clustering quality and scalability, while requiring significantly fewer constraints. Code is available at: https://github.com/BZhXuang/ACMDG_CIKM2026

title: FAIR-PIVOT: Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion for Mitigating Political Bias in Web Corpora
abstract: Large-scale web corpora (e.g., C4) are severely imbalanced in terms of political perspective: on the death penalty issue, e.g., left-leaning documents outnumber right-leaning ones by more than 8-fold. Such imbalances can transfer to downstream large language models, reinforcing political bias. We propose Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion (simply, FAIR-PIVOT), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based two-level-agent framework that builds balanced perspective-inverted synthetic data for politically sensitive topics. After annotating web texts with multi-persona LLMs, FAIR-PIVOT retrieves documents from contrasting orientations and inverts their viewpoint, preserving authentic discourse structure rather than rephrasing the same-view text. Across nine topics, FAIR-PIVOT generates 13,954 instances and reduces the total variation distance, a measure of how far the orientation distribution deviates from uniform balance, by up to 83%, while improving linguistic fluency as measured by Perplexity (25.5 → 21.8 ↓). Fine-tuning small language models on the balanced corpus further shifts their downstream behavior toward the intended orientation (Gemma (L--R)% +48 → +34, Qwen +55 → +50), confirming that data-level balancing can yield fairer model responses. Code and scripts are available at https://github.com/bigbases/FAIR-PIVOT.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Address Linkage in Tracking Ecosystems via Large Language Models
abstract: User tracking aims to identify network activities belonging to the same user across websites and network environments, supporting applications such as personalized recommendation and targeted advertising. As dynamic address allocation and modern privacy protections constrain traditional tracking methods, traffic-based tracking techniques have emerged to link dynamic addresses through traffic patterns. However, existing methods usually rely on large-scale user labels for supervised training, while such labels are difficult to obtain in TLS encrypted traffic, severely limiting model generalization. In this paper, we propose SLATE, a self-supervised address linkage framework integrated with LLMs under limited labeled data. Specifically, SLATE introduces a homologous subgraph discrimination task based on address behavior partitioning, which encourages the encoder to capture stable behavior patterns across temporal evolution from large-scale unlabeled data. Moreover, SLATE develops a graph semantic projection module, which enables the LLM to better interpret behavior graph representations through graph-text matching and node semantic classification, and further leverages its reasoning capability to support address linkage decisions. We evaluate SLATE on two real-world user datasets. Experimental results show that SLATE substantially outperforms the strongest self-supervised methods, achieving an average improvement of over 15% in Hits@1, while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art supervised methods. These findings demonstrate the strong potential of combining self-supervised learning with LLMs for address linkage in tracking ecosystems.

title: Co-JDPRec: Collaborative Joint Dynamic Pruning for Efficient LLM-based Generative Recommendation
abstract: Generative recommendation leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to model item semantics and user preference dynamics through sequence-to-token generation, but deep Transformer layers and wide Feed Forward Network (FFN) dimensions introduce substantial memory and latency overhead in online recommendation scenarios. Existing LLM pruning methods are mainly designed to preserve general language modeling ability, often overlooking the recommendation-specific states shaped by item semantics, collaborative signals, and temporal preference dynamics. To address this limitation, we propose Co-JDPRec, a collaborative joint dynamic pruning framework that shifts the pruning objective from parameter removal to recommendation-state preservation. Specifically, Co-JDPRec introduces a task-aware saliency criterion that combines collaborative alignment and sequence-order sensitivity, enabling the model to identify neurons critical for user-item relations and evolving preference dynamics. Guided by this saliency, Co-JDPRec jointly searches FFN width and layer depth to derive a compact heterogeneous architecture, followed by distillation recovery to restore recommendation performance. Theoretically, Co-JDPRec characterizes structural importance via first-order Taylor sensitivity under recommendation-aware objectives. Empirically, it achieves superior accuracy–efficiency trade-offs on both title-based and semantic-ID-based generative recommendation backbones, validating the effectiveness of recommendation-state-aware pruning.

title: E²L³AE: End-to-End Text Encoder Tuning for LLM-Enhanced Linear Autoencoders
abstract: Enriching sparse user–item interactions with semantic item knowledge is essential for robust recommendation, particularly for long-tail items where collaborative signals are weak or unreliable. L³AE integrates frozen LLM embeddings into linear autoencoders, but fixed text representations can be suboptimal for recommendation because consumption-relevant item characteristics often deviate from general textual semantics. We propose an end-to-end extension that fine-tunes the text encoder within the same linear autoencoder framework, encouraging its embeddings to reflect item relatedness derived from user–item interactions, thereby adapting pretrained textual knowledge to recommendation objectives while remaining grounded in pretrained semantic knowledge. Experiments on public datasets show that our end-to-end trained hybrid model improves upon the original L³AE and other baselines. Moreover, the fine?tuned encoder alone serves as a competitive semantic?based recommender.

title: CoRe-Rec: Budgeted Consistency Policy Re-Rolling for Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Real-time sequential recommendation requires policies that are both expressive and efficient. Diffusion policies can model diverse user preferences, but their iterative denoising process introduces high serving latency. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) actors usually execute a single sampled action without checking whether the action is likely to trigger a positive user response before exposure. We propose CoRe-Rec, a budgeted consistency-policy re-rolling framework for RL-based slate recommendation. CoRe-Rec uses a shared consistency actor to generate continuous hyper-actions in one or few denoising steps. Each hyper-action induces a provisional slate through top-K item scoring. Before execution, a frozen user response model (URM) evaluates multiple low-cost candidates generated with different sampler configurations and noise seeds, and an early-stopping rule selects the best slate under an inference budget. The re-rolling step is a detached test-time search procedure: gradients are not propagated through the discrete sampler selection or the top-K slate construction; instead, the selected branch is recomputed for actor-critic learning. Experiments in simulated environments built from RL4RS, BookCrossing, and MovieLens 1M show that CoRe-Rec improves cumulative reward and episode depth while providing a favorable reward--latency trade-off.

title: Interpretation-Aware Image Manipulation Detection
abstract: Image manipulation has been a common practice since the early days of photography, and has evolved into a sophisticated threat with the rise of powerful image editing tools and generative AI. It can be used to spread misinformation, manipulate public opinion, and cause harm to individuals and communities. In this article, we study the problem of determining whether an image is misleading, i.e. edited in a misleading way. We introduce a risk framework to assess the intrinsic interpretive shift (ITS) of an ordered image pair, which evaluates whether the final edited image changes the interpretation supported by a source reference image. We show our risk framework can be operationalized with the Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) provenance framework. We estimate ITS with a single-call vision-language implementation of our risk framework, which first checks for meaningful visual differences, then tests whether the differences induce interpretive shift, and finally determines whether the shift is fully explained by permissible transformations rather than content-level changes. The system outputs a binary label (potentially misleading or not) together with interpretive clues and a short justification. To test the approach and show that ITS is a measurable proxy for misleading edits, we built a benchmark of 418 ordered pairs, drawn from real-world fact-check cases and meaning-preserving transformations. The best-performing model configuration (gpt-5.4) achieves 88.2% precision, 94.2% recall, and 96.5% balanced accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/liyu0x/ITS_detection/.
